Principium Cognoscendi
prin-KIP-ee-uhm kog-noh-SHEN-dee
doctrinal phrase
Latin, “the principle of knowing”; a term of Reformed scholastic theology for the foundation of the knowledge of God.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Principium cognoscendi—Latin for “the principle of knowing”—is a term of Reformed scholastic theology for the foundation or first principle by which the knowledge of God is obtained. The Reformed divines distinguished the principium essendi, the principle of being, which is God Himself, the source of all that is and of all truth; and the principium cognoscendi, the principle of knowing, which is the way that knowledge of God comes to us. They further distinguished the external principle of knowing, which is Holy Scripture, the inspired Word in which God has revealed Himself; and the internal principle, which is the illumination of the Holy Spirit, by whom the truth of the Word is savingly understood and received. The point of the term is foundational and far-reaching: theology does not begin from human reason, philosophy, experience, tradition, or the church, but from the self-revelation of God in His Word. God is known only because He has made Himself known, and supremely in the Scriptures; reason and experience are servants that follow, never the foundation that grounds. The dictionary commends the doctrine of the principium cognoscendi as a precise statement of the formal principle of the Reformation—Scripture alone as the source and rule of the knowledge of God—against every system that grounds theology in autonomous reason, mystical experience, or ecclesiastical authority. The believer knows God truly because God has spoken in His Word and the Spirit has opened his understanding; the foundation of all sound theology is not what man finds out but what God reveals, received by faith through the Spirit-illumined Scriptures.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

“The principle of knowing”—the Reformed scholastic term for the foundation of the knowledge of God: Scripture as the external principle, the Spirit’s illumination as the internal, against reason or experience as the ground.

PRINCIPIUM COGNOSCENDI, Latin for “the principle of knowing.”

The foundation by which the knowledge of God is obtained.

The external principle is Holy Scripture, God’s self-revelation.

The internal principle is the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Theology begins from God’s revelation, not from reason, experience, or tradition.

📖 Key Scripture

2Ti 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

1Co 2:14 — "But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

Psa 36:9 — "For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light."

Mat 11:27 — "All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Theology is grounded in autonomous reason, experience, or church authority, rather than in God’s self-revelation in Scripture.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the knowledge of God begins from God’s self-revelation, not from man. The external principle of knowing is Holy Scripture, the inspired Word; the internal principle is the Spirit’s illumination, by which the natural man, who cannot receive the things of God, is enabled to discern them. Against every system that grounds theology in autonomous human reason, in mystical experience, or in the authority of the church, the Reformed doctrine confesses that God is known only because and only as He has made Himself known in His Word.

The corruption takes many forms. Rationalism makes human reason the foundation and judge of revelation; mysticism makes inner experience the source of the knowledge of God; Rome makes the church and its tradition the ground and rule. Each displaces the true principium cognoscendi. The dictionary holds the Reformation’s formal principle: Scripture alone is the source and rule of the knowledge of God, illumined by the Spirit who inspired it. Reason and experience are servants that follow the Word, never the foundation that grounds it. The believer knows God truly not by what he finds out but by what God reveals, received by faith through the Spirit-opened Scriptures.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The term names Scripture and the Spirit’s illumination as the foundation of the knowledge of God, against reason or experience as the ground.

expand to see more

Latin principium cognoscendi — “the principle of knowing.”

Distinguished from principium essendi, the principle of being (God Himself).

The external principle: Holy Scripture, God’s self-revelation.

The internal principle: the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

A precise statement of the Reformation’s formal principle, sola Scriptura.

Usage

"The principium cognoscendi names the foundation of the knowledge of God."

"It distinguishes Scripture (external) and the Spirit’s illumination (internal)."

"It is set against grounding theology in reason, experience, or church authority."
